svg.aria-label: Diagram: the three tiers of Google Cloud VPC route by who controls them, the non-removable routes for Google control planes including IAP, Cloud DNS, Serverless VPC Access, Chrome Enterprise Premium and health check return paths with their address ranges, why deleting the default route does not break any of those, and two behaviours that surprise operators: eventually consistent route propagation and routes appearing without action
svg.title: Routes: the tier you own, the tier Google manages, and the tier you cannot see
svg.text: Routes come in three tiers: yours, Google’s but visible, and ones you cannot see at all.
The invisible tier is why deleting the default route does not break health checks or SSH.
Who controls which routes
YOURS — custom routes. Static ones you write; dynamic ones Cloud Router adds and removes
from BGP. Evaluated last, after policy-based routes and after subnet routes.
GOOGLE’S AND VISIBLE — subnet routes, created automatically for each subnet IP range
and removed automatically during subnet lifecycle events. They apply to the whole network.
THE DEFAULT ROUTE — 0.0.0.0/0 to default-internet-gateway. Visible, and CAN BE REMOVED.
The tier you cannot see or delete
Every VPC network carries non-removable routes for Google’s own control planes:
IAP for TCP forwarding — 35.235.240.0/20. This is what SSH and RDP ride.
Cloud DNS and Service Directory private routing — 35.199.192.0/19.
Serverless VPC Access — 35.199.224.0/19. Chrome Enterprise Premium — 136.124.16.0/20.
Health checks and GFE backends — 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22, as return paths.
None is a route you manage. None can be removed. None may be used as a subnet range.
Which is what makes locking down egress safe
Deleting the default route is supported, and is how you force egress through NAT or a proxy.
What does NOT break, because none of it depends on that route:
Load balancing — forwarding rule routing paths do not depend on a default route or on the
default internet gateway next hop. Health checks, IAP SSH and Cloud DNS forwarding all ride
the non-removable paths above. What DOES break is general outbound internet access.
Two behaviours worth knowing before you debug one
ROUTE CHANGES ARE EVENTUALLY CONSISTENT. Add or delete a route and the change propagates
to the per-VM controllers by an eventually consistent design — not to every VM at once.
ROUTES APPEAR WITHOUT YOU. Expanding a primary IPv4 range changes a subnet route, and when
Google adds a region an auto mode network gains a subnet — and therefore a route.
A dynamic route also vanishes on its own when its next hop becomes inaccessible.
Subnet route destinations must be unique across local, peering and NCC subnet routes — so a
peer you add later can be refused by a range you chose today. The same shape as #63 and #65.
The routing table you can list is not the routing table in effect. Three tiers exist; one is
documented only in prose, and it is the one holding up SSH, health checks and DNS.
